agreement.title: The ambassador agreement.

sections.p: You and The Upskilling Labs. You're volunteering as an ambassador: you're not staff, and there's no pay.
Have real conversations with people you know, tell your own story, and invite them to one dated next step. When you're ready, give one short talk to a room. Bring someone new along.

Use the guide's words. Describe our legal status exactly as the guide says it. Never promise jobs, pay, or outcomes, and never speak for The Labs to the press or officials without asking your coordinator first.
You don't collect anyone's contact details for The Labs. People Join The Labs themselves at theupskillinglabs.org.
Our Code of Conduct applies to ambassadors everywhere you represent The Labs, online and in person.
You can stop any time. Tell your coordinator, and you're always welcome back. If an ambassador breaks this agreement or the Code of Conduct, we may ask them to step back.
This is a plain-language summary. The Upskilling Labs' Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, and Code of Conduct govern in full.

video.title: The Labs in three minutes.
video.lede: Watch it, or read the short version. The ten questions come from this.
read: Most people find The Labs because someone they know said “come with me.”

The Labs is free. Workshops, Build Cycles, all of it. Run by volunteers. It grew out of a fall 2025 pilot run by DC Public Library and Levy, a strategic design firm, for about 50 ex-feds navigating career change and new technology. The pilot's alums founded The Labs in January 2026.
The tagline: “Find your people. Build your edge.” The idea behind it: AI is rewriting how we work, and it's easier to learn together than alone.
You don't need a technical background. Just a willingness to learn by doing alongside others.

A Build Cycle is twelve weeks, four a year: Problem Discovery, then Experimentation, then Synthesis. Small teams called pods form around the problems people vote for. Everything built is open-source by default.
Workshops teach two kinds of skills. Durable skills, like communication, storytelling, and framing problems. And AI skills, like prompt engineering and building agents.
Signing in uses a Google account for your name, email, and profile picture only. Never Gmail, Drive, or Calendar.
Your job is three moves. Ask what they're working toward. Share thirty seconds of your story. Invite them to one dated next step.
You don't sell, sign anyone up, or promise a job. People Join The Labs themselves at theupskillinglabs.org.
If anyone asks what we are: “a fiscally sponsored project of Superbloom Design, a 501(c)(3). Our own status is pending.”

quiz.title: Ten questions about The Labs.
quiz.lede: You're here because you lived The Labs and liked what you found. Eight of ten and you're set. It's not about being perfect, it's about being ready to tell the story. Try as often as you like.
quiz.passed: You passed. You're ready to tell the story.
quiz.failed: Not yet. Look again at the ones marked, then try again.

questions.q: What is the tagline of The Upskilling Labs?
options: Find your people. Build your edge.
Learn fast. Work smart.
The future of work, today.
Skills for a changing world.
questions.hint: It has two short parts: one about community, one about skills.
questions.why: “Find your people. Build your edge.” It captures both sides: the community (find your people) and the skills (build your edge).

questions.q: What is the central idea behind why The Labs exists?
options: AI is rewriting how we work, and it's easier to learn together than alone
Traditional universities are too expensive
Remote work has made networking impossible
Certifications are the fastest path to a new job
questions.hint: It's about a big shift in work, and doing something about it together.
questions.why: The Labs is built on the belief that AI is changing work, and learning it alongside people near you beats going it alone.

questions.q: How long is a Build Cycle, and how many run per year?
options: Twelve weeks, 4 cycles per year
Six weeks, 6 cycles per year
One year, 1 cycle per year
Eight weeks, 3 cycles per year
questions.hint: Three months long, once a quarter.
questions.why: A Build Cycle runs twelve weeks, and there are four a year, roughly one per quarter.

questions.q: What are the three phases of a Build Cycle, in order?
options: Problem Discovery → Experimentation → Synthesis
Research → Building → Launch
Onboarding → Workshops → Graduation
Ideation → Funding → Demo
questions.hint: You start by finding a problem and end by synthesizing a working prototype.
questions.why: Month 1 is Problem Discovery, Month 2 is Experimentation, and Month 3 is Synthesis. Each ends with a meetup, capped by a public showcase.

options: A small team that forms around a compelling problem
A weekly workshop session
The physical space at the library where members meet
A subscription tier for members
questions.hint: It's a group of people, not a place or a plan.
questions.why: After community voting surfaces the most compelling problems, small teams called pods form around them to explore and prototype solutions.

questions.q: Do you need a technical background to join The Labs?
options: No. You just need a willingness to learn by doing alongside others
Yes. At least one year of coding experience is required
Yes. A college degree in a STEM field is required
Only for the Build Cycles, not the workshops
questions.hint: The whole point is that it's open to everyone.
questions.why: No technical background is needed. The Labs is peer-powered and project-based, open to anyone willing to learn by doing.

questions.q: What two broad categories of skills does The Labs teach?
options: Durable (human) skills and AI (technical) skills
Coding skills and design skills
Leadership skills and sales skills
Beginner skills and advanced skills
questions.hint: One set is timeless and human; the other is about working with AI.
questions.why: Durable skills are the human ones: communication, storytelling, problem framing. AI skills are the technical side: LLMs, prompt engineering, vibe coding, building agents.

questions.q: Where did The Upskilling Labs start?
options: In a DC Public Library pilot, run with the strategic design firm Levy, whose alums founded The Labs
In Silicon Valley, as a startup accelerator
Online during the pandemic in 2020
At a university in Baltimore
questions.hint: A library, the nation's capital, and a group of former federal workers.
questions.why: It began as a fall 2025 pilot run by DC Public Library and Levy, a strategic design firm, for about 50 ex-feds navigating career change and new technology. The alums of that pilot founded The Upskilling Labs in January 2026.
questions.$comment: Dates confirmed: the pilot ran in fall 2025; the organisation was founded in January 2026.

questions.q: What happens to the work participants create during a Build Cycle?
options: It's open-source by default, so others can learn from and build on it
It's kept private and owned by The Labs
It's sold to sponsors to fund the program
It's deleted at the end of each cycle
questions.hint: Think about the phrase “built in the open.”
questions.why: Everything created is open-source by default (MIT code, CC BY 4.0 content). Even The Labs' own playbooks are built in the open.

questions.q: Why does The Labs ask you to sign in with a Google account?
options: To use only your name, email, and profile picture. Never your Gmail, Drive, or Calendar
To scan your emails for networking opportunities
To sync your Google Calendar with all events
To back up your project files to Google Drive
questions.hint: It's the privacy-conscious answer: minimal access only.
questions.why: Sign-in uses only your name, email, and profile picture, to set up your profile and keep you signed in. The Labs never ask for Gmail, Drive, or Calendar access. A good privacy point to reassure people.
